title: From Proxy to Platform: Building a Multi-Tenant AI Gateway
tldr: Adobe built a shared, multi-tenant LLM gateway on LiteLLM, with its own control plane (console) for self-service model onboarding, fallbacks, budgets and logs. The talk walks through the stages from shared keys to team tenants, agent-driven usage and platform guarantees, and where they go next.

key_points.text: Before the gateway, teams shared long-lived provider keys or ran their own proxies, so nobody could say who used a key, what was spent per app, or whether proxies were patched.
The data plane is LiteLLM, an OpenAI-compatible proxy with routing, fallbacks, auth, rate limits and budget checks; the team's work is the console control plane around it.
When a second team arrived, each team got its own model deployments in its own cloud accounts, reachable only with team-scoped keys, so access and costs never mix.
A tenant is a team, not a user, because use cases, service IDs and budgets belong to teams while people move between teams. Team admins self-serve models, fallback rules and budgets.
Internal agents minted and deleted keys almost every turn, escaping key-based budgets. The fix: stamp the owning human on every key and reconcile agent spend back to that person's budget.

For customer-facing agents, internal apps pass a customer ID via trusted headers or token claims, and the gateway enforces per-customer budgets and limits. A default budget is required, or customers get unlimited spend.
Every request is attributed through tags minted into the key, so callers never send them per request.
Platform guarantees: tested fallbacks on every upgrade, scaling on in-flight requests instead of CPU, and provider alerts that reach tenants rather than being swallowed.
Upgrades flow dev, stage, prod via GitOps pull requests with a seven-day cooldown after a prod regression and API contract tests; CVE fixes skip the cooldown and ship the same day.

On Kubernetes: isolated namespaces with network policies, no keys in pods, tenant IAM roles, KEDA scaling on in-flight requests, PodDisruptionBudgets, long drain grace periods, Argo CD sync and rollback, and one Helm chart per region.
Next: multi-region with full in-region stacks for data residency, tenant-defined auto routing with evals to check cost/quality, and moving from keys to agent and workload identity.

numbers.text: Seven-day cooldown between dev and prod promotion for new LiteLLM versions.
The infrastructure team runs hundreds of clusters across clouds.

open_gaps.text: Data residency requires running the whole stack in one region, and not every provider offers every model in every region, so fallback config must also be region-bound. Still in design.
Keys still carry budgets and attribution; replacing them with agent identity tied to internal identity systems or Kubernetes service accounts is longer term.
Auto routing is only in pilot; tenants need a way to prove it gives the cost/quality tradeoff they want.

opportunities.text: Stamp an owning human or customer ID on every gateway key and enforce default budgets so agent-minted keys cannot bypass limits.
Autoscale LLM proxies on in-flight requests with KEDA instead of CPU.
Add API contract tests and a cooldown stage to your gateway upgrade pipeline, with a fast path for CVE fixes.
Describe a maturity model for your own AI gateway using the stages here: shared keys, team tenants, agents, platform guarantees.
